# A genuinely critical, nonheavy 3+2 source with nonconvex folded Ball body
Ball obstruction by retaining strictly nonheavy fibers. It refutes the
convexity of this one-sided sampled fold's Ball body, not OC. the contributor
supplied the fold mechanism; the parameters and uniform cap lower bound
below give the no-heavy repair.

## 1. Exact actual convex source

Let T=conv((0,0),(1,0),(0,1)), g=(1/3,1/3), and eps=1/5. Put

    A=eps T,       |A|=1/50,
    Q=2/9+1/50=109/450.

Let u=(1,1)/sqrt(2), v=(1,-1)/sqrt(2), and define the centrally
symmetric rectangle

    R=2g+[-3/10,3/10]u+[-109/270,109/270]v.            (1)

Its area is

    |R|=4(3/10)(109/270)=109/225=2Q.                  (2)

At integer bases -1,0,1 prescribe A,T,R and take the convex hull of
their embedded fibers. Its actual endpoint fibers are A,R. Its middle
fiber is exactly T because (A+R)/2 is contained in T. To check this
last assertion completely, every coordinate of R is at least

    2/3-19/(27 sqrt(2))>0,

and

    max_(a in A,r in R) [(a_1+r_1)+(a_2+r_2)]
          =1/5+4/3+(3/10)sqrt(2)<2.                   (3)

The two strict comparisons follow by squaring positive quantities:
18 sqrt(2)>19 and sqrt(2)<14/9. Nonnegative coordinates and total
coordinate sum at most two are precisely membership in 2T. Thus no
unintended middle-fiber enlargement occurs.

The resulting body C is full-dimensional in R x R^2, and its complete
integer base is {-1,0,1}. Its total mixed area is

    M=1/50+1/2+109/225=226/225.

All three fibers are strictly lighter than M/2=113/225: the largest
has area1/2, and 1/2<113/225. No intrinsic-degeneracy issue arises.

## 2. A uniform right-fiber cap reserve

The rectangle R contains the Euclidean ball of radius3/10 centered at
2g. For every unit direction w, the cap of this ball with
w.(x-2g)>=1/5 has area at least14/625. Indeed choose a perpendicular
unit direction w_perp. The two rectangles with disjoint interiors in
these coordinates

    1/5<=w.(x-2g)<=6/25,  |w_perp.(x-2g)|<=9/50,
    6/25<=w.(x-2g)<=7/25, |w_perp.(x-2g)|<=1/10

lie in the ball. The first has maximal squared radius
(6/25)^2+(9/50)^2=9/100; the second has maximal squared radius
(7/25)^2+(1/10)^2=221/2500<9/100. Their total area is

    (1/25)(9/25)+(1/25)(1/5)=14/625>1/50.             (4)

This is an exact elementary bound uniform over every continuous normal,
not a numerical circular-cap estimate.

## 3. Exact depth and the two genuine deepest contacts

There is a particularly short lower-bound proof using exact reflected
containment. Since A is contained in the ball of radius1/5 at zero and
R contains the ball of radius3/10 at2g,

    2g-A subset R.

The endpoint subsource consisting of A at base -1 and 2g-A at base 1
is centrally symmetric about y_0=(0,g), with total area2|A|. Every
closed through-y_0 ambient halfspace captures at least |A| from this
subsource, including any boundary mass. Every nonvertical such cap
captures at least2/9 from the own T fiber by ordinary Grunbaum; a
vertical cap contains that entire fiber. Thus depth(y_0)>=Q. This
reflection argument does not require the numerical reserve (4).

For completeness, the independently valid reserve argument gives a
second all-direction verification:

Consider y_0=(0,g). Any containing halfspace can first be replaced by
its parallel through-y_0 halfspace. If its continuous normal is nonzero,
normalize it to a unit w and write it as

    w.(x-g)+a z>=0.                                  (5)

The own triangular fiber contributes at least (4/9)|T|=2/9 by ordinary
Grunbaum at g. If (5) contains every point of A at base -1, its mass is
already at least 2/9+1/50=Q. Otherwise there is a_0 in A with

    w.(a_0-g)-a<0.

At the right center 2g the margin is w.g+a>w.a_0>=-eps=-1/5, since
every point of A has Euclidean norm at most eps. Consequently the right
trace of (5) contains the entire ball cap used in (4), and its mass
again exceeds 2/9+1/50. A purely integer through-y_0 closed halfspace
contains the whole middle fiber and hence has mass at least1/2>Q.
This proves depth(y_0)>=Q for ALL ambient halfspaces.

At y_1=(1,2g), every nonvertical containing halfspace captures at least
half of R by central symmetry, namely Q. Every purely integer containing
halfspace contains the entire R fiber. Thus depth(y_1)>=Q as well.

For an exact upper bound and a genuine 3+2 critical cover, use the three
canonical triangular caps through y_0 with a common isolating tilt:

    H_1={x_1-1/3-10z>=0},
    H_2={x_2-1/3-10z>=0},
    H_3={-x_1-x_2+2/3-10z>=0}.                        (6)

Each captures all of A, exactly area2/9 in T, and none of R, so each
has mass Q. The last assertion is strict: all coordinates of R have
absolute value less than2, whereas the tilt is10. Their margins sum to
-30z, so their union covers every continuous plane above z<=0.

At y_1 use the opposite pair

    J_+={x_1-2/3+10(z-1)>=0},
    J_-={-x_1+2/3+10(z-1)>=0}.                        (7)

Each excludes A and T strictly and cuts R into equal halves, so each
has mass Q. They cover every plane above z>=1. The five closed caps
(6)--(7) cover every actual integer fiber. They prove global maximal
raw depth at most Q. Together with the two lower bounds this gives

    max depth raw = Q,
    max depth normalized = Q/M=109/452.                (8)

All five caps are genuinely active at their stated globally deepest
contact. The triple has continuous rank two and positive normal balance;
the pair has continuous rank one and positive balance. The contacts are
actual mixed-integer points, and the full lower bound included oblique
and purely integer halfspaces with their boundary mass.

## 4. The one-sided projective fold and its exact radial defect

Shear the continuous coordinate by subtracting (z+1)g. This is the
single affine shear taking both deepest contacts to continuous zero.
The fibers at bases0 and -1 become respectively

    K_0=T-g,       A.

The one-sided fold about the right contact scales the left fiber by
1/(1-(-1))=1/2 and retains its exact area weight4. Its resulting
ordinary density is therefore

    f=1_(T-g)+4 1_L,        L=A/2=(1/10)T.             (9)

The origin is interior to T-g. The added small triangle L is contained
in T-g. Define its Ball star body about zero by the radial integral,
without assuming that this body is convex. For a nonzero point q its
gauge is

    p_f(q)=[2 integral_0^infinity t f(tq)dt]^(-1/2).    (10)

On the original facet x_1+x_2=1/3 take

    q_1=(2/3,-1/3),
    q_3=(1/6,1/6),
    q_2=(q_1+q_3)/2=(5/12,-1/12).

The rays q_1,q_2 have a negative second coordinate and meet L only at
zero. Their original triangular radial endpoint is t=1, so

    p_f(q_1)=p_f(q_2)=1.

On the ray q_3, membership in L lasts exactly until t=3/10. Thus

    2 integral_0^infinity t f(tq_3)dt
        =1+4(3/10)^2=34/25,
    p_f(q_3)=5/sqrt(34)<1.                            (11)

But q_2 is the midpoint of q_1 and q_3, and

    p_f(q_2)=1>(1+5/sqrt(34))/2.

The gauge of a convex body containing zero would be convex, so this
Ball star body is not convex. All three rays used here avoid the small
triangle's directional boundary except at their zero point; the defect
does not depend on arbitrary density values on a null boundary.

## 5. Precise scope

This counterexample retains actual convex fiber compatibility, a complete
integer base, all positive full-dimensional fibers, strictly nonheavy
fiber masses, two actual globally deepest contacts, and five genuinely
critical original caps in a 3+2 cover. It rules out the assertion that
the indicated one-sided sampled projective fold automatically has a
convex ordinary Ball body under these hypotheses.

The raw depth in (8) is above OC: 109/452>2/9. No bad-minimum assumption
is satisfied. The example therefore does not refute a transfer theorem
with a genuinely additional below-target premise, the new transverse
slab inclusions, or OC itself.
